questions.question: Define a transverse pulse and amplitude, and explain what travels along the spring when a pulse passes and what does not.
questions.expected_answer: A pulse is a single disturbance moving through a medium. In a transverse pulse the particles of the medium move at right angles — perpendicular — to the direction in which the pulse travels: a piece of tape on the spring lifts straight up and sinks straight back while the pulse moves horizontally past it. The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its rest (equilibrium) position, measured in metres from the rest line to the point of greatest displacement — never from a dip to a crest. What travels along the spring is the disturbance and the energy it carries; the medium itself does not travel — every particle makes a short round trip and returns to its rest position. A pulse transfers energy through a medium without transferring the medium itself.

questions.question: State the principle of superposition. A crest of displacement plus 0,4 m meets a trough of displacement minus 0,1 m. Give the resultant displacement at complete overlap, name the type of interference, and describe the pulses afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: The principle of superposition states that when two or more pulses occupy the same point of a medium at the same time, the displacement of the medium at that point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements — added with their signs. Here the resultant is plus 0,4 plus minus 0,1, which is plus 0,3 m: a reduced hump of 0,3 m. Because the pulses displace the medium in opposite directions and the resultant is smaller than the larger pulse, this is destructive interference. After the overlap both pulses pass through each other and continue completely unchanged — each keeps its original shape, amplitude and direction of travel.

questions.question: Two pulses of equal amplitude but opposite displacement overlap and the spring is momentarily flat. Explain why the pulses are not destroyed, and why jerking the spring harder cannot make a pulse travel faster.
questions.expected_answer: At complete overlap the displacements sum to zero at every point, so the spring looks flat, but both pulses still exist: at that instant their energy is stored in the motion — the kinetic energy — of the spring's particles, which are still moving even though their displacement is zero. A moment later the crest emerges on one side and the trough on the other, each with its original amplitude and direction. Flat does not mean gone. Jerking harder only puts more energy into the pulse, which shows up as a larger amplitude. The speed of a pulse is a property of the medium — it depends on the tension in the spring and on its mass — so every pulse on the same spring travels at the same speed regardless of size. Only changing the medium, for example stretching the spring more tightly, changes the speed.
